idiom_name: JVM ServiceLoader / Class.forName + kotlin-reflect constructor lookup
implementation_notes: Kotlin has no dynamic linking of its own; on the JVM it uses class loading exactly as Java does - ServiceLoader for provider discovery (META-INF/services or a module's provides directive), Class.forName/classLoader.loadClass for a component named in configuration - and constructs components reflectively through kotlin-reflect (KClass.constructors / primaryConstructor.callBy) when arguments include default or named parameters, which java.lang.reflect cannot supply. The contract is an interface in a shared artifact loaded by a parent class loader. Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS have no runtime linking at all, so there the composition is compile-time or out-of-process; the classic structure remains justified for JVM hosts that must accept third-party jars at run time.
code_sketch:
val type = Class.forName(cfg.className)        // JVM class loading
val kcls = type.kotlin                          // requires kotlin-reflect
val ctor = kcls.primaryConstructor ?: kcls.constructors.first()
val component = ctor.callBy(ctor.parameters.associateWith { cfg.params[it.name] })
// or, for discovered providers: ServiceLoader.load(ComponentFactory::class.java)
pitfalls: Reflective construction of Kotlin types needs the kotlin-reflect artifact (version-matched to the compiler line); plain java.lang.reflect cannot fill default parameters and fails on Kotlin-specific signatures.

Class identity is the JVM's: if the component loads its own copy of the contract instead of resolving it from a shared parent loader, casts to the host interface fail with ClassCastException/NoClassDefFoundError.

Kotlin maps to its own JVM names (@JvmName, @JvmStatic, companion objects, name-mangled internal members), so the class and method names a configuration names are the JVM ones, not necessarily the Kotlin declarations you see in the source.
